terms.definition: The ceiling- or wall-mounted radio that connects wireless devices to the hospital's wired network.
The family of IEEE standards that defines Wi-Fi. Each generation is an amendment with a letter suffix, such as 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) or 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7).
Small battery-powered tags on staff or equipment that report their location so teams can find pumps, wheelchairs or colleagues quickly.
Continuous wireless monitoring of a patient's vital signs, sent from a bedside or wearable monitor to a central station.
A small wearable communicator that lets clinicians call and message each other hands-free over Wi-Fi.
A Wi-Fi 7 feature that gives one connection links in several bands; depending on the device, it uses them together or switches between them without reconnecting.
How much radio spectrum one Wi-Fi channel occupies. Wider channels carry more data at once, but fewer of them fit in a band.
A device built for an older Wi-Fi generation. Slow devices take longer to send the same data, so they use more of a shared channel’s airtime.
A class of 6 GHz access points limited to indoor use at low power, allowed across the whole US 6 GHz band without a coordination service.
The way Wi-Fi encodes bits into a radio signal. Higher orders, such as 4096-QAM, pack more bits into each signal but need a cleaner, stronger signal.
One of the many narrow frequencies that make up a Wi-Fi channel. Each carries a few bits at a time, in parallel with the others.
The previous generation of Wi-Fi security. Its password-based mode lets a recorded sign-in be attacked offline.
The current generation of Wi-Fi security, with a sign-in that resists offline password guessing and stronger encryption options.
The WPA3 sign-in exchange. Both sides prove they know the password without revealing anything an eavesdropper could test offline.
A property where learning a password later does not let someone decrypt traffic they recorded earlier, because each session used its own key.
An agreement between a device and an access point about when the device will wake up to send or receive, so it can sleep the rest of the time.
An optional Wi-Fi 7 form of Target Wake Time that better protects scheduled slots for latency-sensitive traffic such as voice and telemetry, on devices that support it.
The agreed window of time during which a device wakes to exchange data under a Target Wake Time agreement.
The share of time a channel spends carrying a given device's traffic. Every device on an access point competes for the same airtime.
How long data takes to get from one device to another. For alarms and voice, lower is better.
The raw speed at which bits are sent over the air. Usable throughput is always lower because of protocol overhead and sharing.
An independent data stream sent over its own antenna path at the same time as others. More streams multiply the peak rate.
A bedside pump that delivers medication at a set rate and uses Wi-Fi to receive drug libraries and orders and to report alerts and history.
A bedside or wearable monitor that tracks vital signs such as heart rhythm and oxygen levels and sends readings and alarms to the nurses’ station over Wi-Fi.
A mobile cart with a computer and scanner that clinicians push from room to room to chart, scan medications and look up records over Wi-Fi.
A hospital-managed phone that staff use for calls, secure messages, alarm notifications and barcode scanning over Wi-Fi.
Wi-Fi sign-in with one shared password for every device on the network, common for clinical devices that cannot hold their own credentials.
Wi-Fi sign-in where each person or device uses its own credentials, checked by the hospital’s sign-in server, instead of one shared password.
A rogue radio set up to imitate the hospital network, so devices connect to it and hand over sign-in details or traffic.
